I've always loved the older Resident Evil games, however the last one I actually remember much about was Resident Evil 3 as I owned that one growing up, and only played the previous games at a friend's house.

This Remaster/Remake is just was I was hoping for.  The newer Titles RES 5 and RES 6 focus way too much on action, and you often end up with a small asenal at your disposal with a ridiculous amount of ammo.

This is not the case with this Remaster/Remake.  Ammo is limited, Inventory space is limited, and even your vision is limited depending on where the camera is situated. (this is a good thing)

It makes you use caution when moving somewhere, often you may want to rely on your senses... can you hear a zombie groaning in the other room? or was it just your imagination?


I started out playing this game on hard mode, just to see what it was like.  I died from the 2nd or 3rd zombie I encountered.  It was a brutal experience, the zombies were tough as nails eating most of  clip from my hand gun before finally dying.  

I was stuck relying on my knife almost immediately due to not having enough ammo to take care of the zombies, and since I needed to get around the zombies to proceed, there was little choice.  Due to being in close melee range, it also meant they could grab and eat me.. which is what usually ended up happening.

Hard mode was INTENSE..  It was terrifyingly amazing how useless and weak I felt.  This made me actually FEAR the zombies.  Everytime I entered a new room I was a tense situation not knowing if there would be a zombie to greet me as soon as I stepped though the door..

After a couple of deaths I decided to switch to Easy Mode and progressed through the game much better.
While it was Easy Mode, I still thoroughly enjoyed the experience.  It wasn't a walk in the park, the game was still challenging but the player can take more hits before dying, and there are more healing herbs and ammo scattered around the mansion.  This was greatly benifital to me as I had no idea where I was going, or what I was to expect up ahead and it allowed some room for error.

There were still times where I died, but often it was due to being ill prepared.  There are multiple traps in this game, and while they look like they would probably be insta-death I managed to avoid all of them by being cautious or just seeing ahead.

I finished the game after about 20 or so hours.. This was actually a pretty long play through and could have been done much shorter.  This was widely because of not knowing where I was going.  Not to say that you are wandering around aimlessly.. (although you kind of are in a sense)  There is a map, and its the key to progressing.  Some areas of the mansion are unaccessable until you find a certain objects.. like keys, or items used for puzzles that open way for new areas.

There is a lot of back tracking involved and the game doesn't direct you at all by giving you a marker to move towards or a mission objective to complete.  Its all up to you, and it feels great!

After finishing the game and making sure I had 100% of the map and item progression I decided to check online to see if there was anything else I could unlock or do in the game.  In fact there was.. but I had to play on Hard Mode.


I was still a bit in fear of the experience I had with Hard Mode the first time around, but I decided to come back and try it again a couple of weeks later.


Having learned a lot from playing and finishing the game on Easy Mode, I figured I had a better chance at survival than when I first attemped Hard Mode.

While the zombies were MUCH harder to kill, you take brutal amounts of damage, and ammo was scarce.  I did indeed have a better grip on the game..  I was ready.



Unlocking the Samurai Edge Pistol. (beat the game in under 5 hours)
Unlocking the Anti-Tank Rocket Launcher. (beat the game in under 3 hours)

Given how it took me over 20 hours to beat the game on Easy Mode, I clearly had some work to do if I was going to even get close.


The first thing I did was find out if there were any safe places where the game clock did not tick.. like in a menu, or pausing.. during cut scenes.. etc.  There was not.

The moment you load the game, there is no pausing the timer.. PERIOD.  This means you really have to be careful when you save the game.  Thinking a head is critical, you have to know where you are going and where all the monsters are.

I decided I would do some trial and error with some runs.. I'd take a path, get the items I found to be valuable in order to progress the quickest without having to back track too much.  

The game needs to be done in segments, figure out a path that leads you to get some importent items and then gets you back to your safe house to save/deposit items to clear up your intentory.  Planning was integral to success, as I didn't want to go through the game and fail just short of the required time to get my unlocks. 

My brother and I decided to digitally draw the mansion using mspaint by tracing an online map of the mansion.  I was then able to mark rooms that were locked with a certain key, or needed something special to progress.  Making a path to follow was also easier as you could now visualize the whole processes before going through with it.

Through a lot of trail and error, I completed the game in about 2 hours and 30 minutes.  This was a great success for me, and I unlocked both weapons in one run.  While I finished the game with an in game clock of under 3 hours, in reality it probably took me longer to complete than the first play through since I often was not happy with my segment times and would redo them.


This process turned me into a zombie dodging ninja, as often the fastest way through a room wasn't to clear it by gunning zombies down.. it was to simply step around them somehow.  Completing this time trial challange has essentially turned Hard Mode turned into Easy Mode.. and it was a lot of fun.


The games over now right?  Wrong.

There are 2 characters you can choose to play as.

Chris 
Higher max HP
Higher damage output using a Knife
Starts with the Lighter item

Jill
Larger inventory capacity
Starts with a lock pick

They have different story progressions and you explore the masion taking different paths.

If you finish the game with both Chris and Jill on at least Normal Mode, the next time you play, the game will throw a new zombie into the mix.. This zombie has a bomb straped to it's chest and killing it will result in an explosion that will always kill you.

Not enough?


Invisible Enemy Mode - Yeah.. its what it says, the enemies are invisible.  I haven't even attempted this yet as I am certain how it will turn out...  but one day..

There are also different costumes you can unlock per character.


Lastly.. there are also Steam Achivements to strive for.. like

Beat the game without saving.
Beat the game using only a knife. (no other weapons, not even counter/defensive ones)

I recently decided to play all the mainline Resident Evil games for the first time ever and it was honestly the best decision I have ever made.
I loved Resident Evil 1 so much, the exploration, the vibes, and the atmosphere were just perfect. It gave me a nostalgic feeling for the 90s even though I wasn't born yet.
If you haven't started playing Resident Evil yet, what the hell are you waiting for?

Resident Evil is an incredible, highly replayable, memorable, tense, and beautiful game. And it's really unfortunate that this remaster is kinda... bad. The gorgeous pre-rendered backgrounds of the 2002 GameCube original have been completely destroyed with over-sharpened, blotchy, poorly rendered upscales. There's also an intense contrast filter slapped on top of it that leads to extreme cases of crushed blacks and loss of visual detail. The music plays too fast and is higher pitched than it should be. The mouse cursor doesn't go away. The resolution caps at 1080p and the framerate caps at 60. I also find it crazy that after numerous re-releases, the remake, and the remake's various ports and releases, you're STILL not able to skip the door animations. It's safe to say this remaster is pretty rough.

So, why do I recommend it then? Two things, really. First, the game itself is still amazing, and everyone should play it. Second, there's mods that fix literally every issue I just listed.

The first mod is the most important one, and that is ThirteenAG's Resident Evil Fusion Fix. This mod fixes the resolution and framerate cap, lets you turn off the contrast filter, lets you skip door animations, hides the mouse cursor, and more.

The second mod is RESCALE. This is the current best backgrounds replacement mod the community has to offer, and it works wonders to this game's visuals. The shoddy 2015 upscales done by Capcom are completely overhauled with, albeit somewhat flawed, modern AI upscaling technology, greatly improving visual clarity and detail. This one is a must-have, but it does come with a fairly hefty download.

The last mod is the Normalized Music Mod. This fixes the strangely quiet and sped-up music tracks the game has out of the box.

All these mods are very easy to install, being just simple drag-and-drop replacements of game files, so please, play this game and install these mods, and enter the survival horror.

[h3]Full Circle[/h3]
Finally, it has come full circle! The original game made me who I am today - a compulsive hoarder. Only in virtual worlds, thankfully. I was so traumatized by all the panic and creature horror, but most of all - the inventory horror! Unprecedented for the time, the scarcity angle caught me off guard, and, for better or worse, it was never repeated to the same degree within the main series. To this day, I always have oodles of consumables left unused in any RPG, boast Amazon storages of ammunition in shooters, and I've beaten Silent Hill 2 into submission by primarily using a nail board. Bless your shivering, shrieking core, PTSD! Here I am, sinking my teeth into the necrotic pudding once more. Rich and creamy.

In the light of what I just said, it may sound weird, but RE sort of calms me down. There's no other way - you pull yourself together or get pulled apart. Collected, I tune in to its rhythmic pacing and calculated tension. I soak in the atmosphere, flow with the ambiance, and appreciate how the game treats its ripe horror tropes. While my love for Silent Hill is high-functioning, cerebral, what I feel for this franchise is visceral, almost carnal. Undeniably, I'm a die-hard fan. The last time I could call myself a fan happily, I was playing Fallout 2 while listening to Chocolate Starfish and the Hot Dog Flavored Water. But it's coming back now, it's coming back. Happiness, not Limp Bizkit.

[h3]Story & Puzzles[/h3]
I suppose I need to start this thing off properly with the game's story? I don't even think I need to give you my take on it. Who gives a crap about my thoughts on Mozart, for example? Okay, here you go: virus bad, Barry is my hunny bunny, mansion traps, monsters Cronenberg, your inventory is full, Salieri was falsely accused and then the fallacy was sung by poets for drama points. Not that sophisticated of a premise by modern standards, but a trendsetting classic nonetheless. I would never think of adding or subtracting anything like I wouldn't change a thing about a cat. Here, the golden cheese of outlandish voice acting got fixed, however, the old one remains out there forever, so I don't mind.

With a few notable exceptions, backtracking-intensive puzzles boil down to "I can't wait to get rid of this thing to save up some inventory space" kinds of entente. To boot, every so often, you're welcome to die after failing to figure out the logic behind a strict sequence of steps to perform on the double. No hard feelings though. Each time I inserted another object into another slot and heard the satisfying *click* or took the right course of action, it echoed inside my weary soul. I made some progress, I freed up some space, I lived, after all! Indulging an important relieving pause, my mind starts racing again, I'm on the move. I definitely saw a herb and some sweet shotgun ammo during my last impetuous scamper through the eastern wing.

[h3]They See Me Turnin', They Hatin'[/h3]
The remake has added an "Alternative" movement type as an option, but I initially went for tank controls anyway. The keyboard lends itself fine to this scheme, this is how I played the original. Yeah, yeah, you can't just lounge back and enjoy yourself while playing, but I'm okay with hunching like a true nerd. Tank controls have their charm, even some nostalgic value to me. Besides, horror only gets juicier the more uncomfortable it makes you feel... so I told myself until I finally found a spare mini-USB adapter, plugged in my gamepad, and tried the alternative. What can I say? Nothing beats instant turning, tank controls have no chance against such an obscene advantage! Although, they deserve to be honored for serving us faithfully - like horses before the age of cars or spittoons before the age of swallowing our phlegm.

[h3]I Love Fixed Camera Angles[/h3]
Speaking of paradigm shifts, they did a number on this remake's presentation. The competent use of dynamic lighting and crisp shadows makes certain moments even more dreadful than before, and locations - even more memorable, despite being somewhat drained of color. The detailed body horror of smooth models, headsplosions, and grimy pre-rendered backgrounds look fantastic, getting emphasized by the cinematic camera. In professional hands, dramatic camera angles really tie it all together! Nothing can set things up and create meticulously controlled experiences for a player quite as they do. And thanks to them, the perfect 80's horror sets that are this mansion's intricate, interconnected environments are the scariest character in the game.

Remember the room where you see a zombie around the corner in a mirror or these infamous hallways with cracking windows? Such well-manipulated scares! And you don't always need a threat for things to get eerie - like with these menacing staircase shots snatched directly from Alone in the Dark. Creating tension where there isn't a thing otherwise (as yet) and sustaining it is high art where, needless to say, the masterful sound design does half the job. Sure, clutch angles also cause such jarring issues as obstructing your vision when it's least appropriate, ending up with you getting blindsided by something that your character should've noticed from a mile away. I brush it off by saying that beauty requires sacrifice and sometimes it's chunks of your face.

[h3]On Curve[/h3]
You know what would be dakka? To just push-kick a zombie. Could one possibly catch your foot? Then again, hit too hard and you'll get stuck in its rotting guts. Zombie theories! Many of us are wired to always loop back to those in moments of respite. Anyway, it took me a while to learn how to evade properly, and even then, I wasn't exactly a floating butterfly, so I died a lot. In RE, however, losing a whole hour of progress is not a huge tragedy since redoing everything in a more efficient way is a treat in itself. To a degree. It's a genuinely hard game full of devious beginner's traps. After 3 hours of rapidly snowballing collapse, I swallowed my pride and restarted on medium difficulty, amply lubing the inverted difficulty curve.

Even with the new controls and the addition of defensive items seen in recent remakes, the game stays challenging, which is appreciated by veterans and amateurs alike. As for me, I'm happy with my humble "easy" victory for which poor Jill had to die a thousand deaths. I can't say I'm dying to experience an even smaller inventory, so, Chris, my apologies. Jill is the one who's packing. But enough about dying! Killing here is pleasant... and punitive. So cathartic, gory, fairly gratuitous, though simultaneously discouraged by sensible ammo shortage and fast Crimson Head zombies who start spawning later in the game from the bodies you made, but didn't burn or decapitate. It sounds like a nuisance, but no enemy is worse than dogs and birds anyway, trust me. The same goes for their in-game counterparts.

Being restricted and weak lends itself to the genre perfectly. Resident Evil knows how to play these cards expertly, it's confident enough to make you cooperate on its terms. I loved every predicament that it put me through! Making someone enjoy a thing they predictably would is admirable, but to think up mechanics that are repelling on paper and make them work in that someone's best interests I call pure brilliance. Every time you have to leave the safe room, you feel the taste of iron in your mouth, lick your lips that suddenly went dry. Thrilled, you tense up, wondering if you have the willpower for the constricting adventure howling in the corridors beyond. Inhale. Clench that shotgun, focus your senses. Turn the knob. Exhale. Run back in because you forgot to put the damn ink ribbons into the box.

[b]Resident Evil HD Remaster breathes new life into the original survival horror masterpiece that started it all. This updated version of the 1996 classic doesn't just polish the visuals, it elevates the entire experience while maintaining the core elements that made the original so iconic. For fans of the genre and newcomers alike, this remaster offers an unforgettable journey into the Spencer Mansion's terrifying corridors.[/b]

[h1]A Return to Survival Horror’s Roots[/h1]
[b]The remaster revisits the classic story of Resident Evil, where players step into the shoes of either Chris Redfield or Jill Valentine, members of the elite S.T.A.R.S. team, sent to investigate mysterious murders on the outskirts of Raccoon City. What follows is a horrifying descent into the heart of the Spencer Mansion, a labyrinth of secrets, puzzles, and grotesque monstrosities.
The game stays true to its roots, focusing on tension, resource management, and environmental storytelling. Even after all these years, the mansion is as haunting and enigmatic as ever.[/b]

[h1]Enhanced Visuals and Atmosphere[/h1]
[b]The updated graphics in the HD Remaster are a standout feature. The pre-rendered backgrounds are beautifully remastered, with enhanced lighting and textures bringing the creepy atmosphere of the Spencer Mansion to life. Shadows flicker, lightning illuminates the dark hallways, and every creak of the floorboards feels more immersive than ever.
The game’s sound design is another highlight, with eerie background music and haunting ambient noises adding to the tension. It’s a game that demands to be played with headphones for the full effect.[/b]

[h1]Refined Controls: Old and New[/h1]
[b]One of the biggest improvements is the addition of modernized controls. The tank controls of the original, while still available for purists, are now complemented by an alternative control scheme that feels more fluid and intuitive. This makes the game more accessible for new players while preserving the challenge and suspense that defined the original.[/b]

[h1]Puzzles and Exploration: Engaging and Rewarding[/h1]
[b]The remaster retains the intricate puzzles and exploration that were a hallmark of the original. From cryptic riddles to hidden keys, each discovery feels satisfying and rewarding. The layout of the mansion itself is a puzzle, with shortcuts, locked doors, and secret pathways that gradually reveal themselves as you progress.[/b]

[h1]Survival Horror at Its Best[/h1]
[b]Resident Evil HD Remaster captures the essence of survival horror. Resources like ammunition and healing items are scarce, forcing players to make strategic choices and manage their inventory carefully. Every encounter with a zombie or monstrous creature feels tense and consequential, with death always lurking around the corner.
The addition of Crimson Heads, zombies that can resurrect into faster, deadlier versions if not disposed of properly, adds a new layer of fear and strategy, ensuring that even areas you thought were “safe” remain a source of dread.[/b]

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*]Stunning visual overhaul: Pre-rendered backgrounds and lighting effects look gorgeous and atmospheric.
[*]Refined controls: The addition of modern controls makes the game more accessible.
[*]Classic survival horror: Maintains the tension, resource management, and puzzle-solving that define the genre.
[*]Improved sound design: Creepy ambient noises and music enhance the eerie atmosphere.
[*]Faithful to the original: Captures the essence of what made the original Resident Evil a masterpiece.
[*]Crimson Heads: A chilling new twist to the zombie threat.
[*]Multiple playthroughs encouraged: With two characters (Chris and Jill), different endings, and challenging modes, replayability is high.
[/list]
[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*]Fixed camera angles: While iconic, they can feel dated to some players and make combat tricky.
[*]Limited inventory space: Adds to the challenge but can be frustrating at times.
[*]Pace may feel slow: The deliberate pacing and backtracking might not appeal to players unfamiliar with older games.
[*]No major story changes: Veterans of the original may find little new content in terms of narrative.
[*]Lack of accessibility options: Limited features for modern accessibility standards.
[/list]
[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
[b]Resident Evil HD Remaster is a masterclass in remaking a classic. It preserves the charm and terror of the original while improving on its visuals, controls, and overall presentation. This is survival horror at its finest, with a haunting atmosphere, engaging puzzles, and relentless tension that keeps you on the edge of your seat.
For longtime fans, it’s a nostalgic trip back to the Spencer Mansion with a fresh coat of paint. For newcomers, it’s a fantastic way to experience one of gaming’s most influential titles. Despite a few dated mechanics, the remaster is a must-play for anyone looking to explore the roots of survival horror. Just remember: in the world of Resident Evil, every bullet and every step matters.[/b]

I imagine that every time a new Resident Evil game comes out, there will be new fans wondering if they should play this remake of the game that started it all. Considering how low the percentage is on some of the mid and late game achievements, it’s evident that it’s not easy for everyone to stick it out to the end. So why is that? 

Put simply, the game is very unfair on the first run and I even considered giving up out of frustration. I put the game down out of annoyance the year before too, so this was a pattern. I made the mistake of playing as Chris for my first run on Medium (what it considers easy) knowing that it would be harder so I could do a victory lap with Jill on the hardest skill available afterwards. While my thinking wasn’t entirely terrible, playing as Chris for the first run is an absolute chore. The backtracking became ever constant, and I say this as someone that has had experience in all the other RE games and some indie survival horrors. Only take what you need and don’t bring extra ammo unless you’re going to a boss fight. Combat itself is not difficult once you get used to the controls. 
Even when I played as Jill on the Normal difficulty - adding many more zombies and kerosene necessities to the run, I only died maybe twice across both playthroughs to actual combat. Once was getting knocked off a ledge by Lisa Trevor, and another was getting pecked to death by crows when I was low on health. You are much more likely to die from the stressful puzzle sequences that will result in your demise if you don’t do something or just press a random button out of curiosity. 

So don’t be ashamed to look at a walkthrough, because I certainly needed the help every once in a while. Like I didn’t understand the need to stop a waterfall, or have the patience to do a chemical mixing puzzle with lots of math. I’d say if you’re also wanting to go to the original RE to witness another fun, fleshed out story like some of the other remakes - just watch a lore recap on YouTube. The script in this game is terrible and left me pretty disappointed as a fan of all the games, even the bad ones. It might not be PS1 levels of hilarious, but now it’s so stilted, inconsistent and borderline nonsensical. 

It might sound like I hate this game, so why still put it in Recommended? Well there’s something to say for a game still being interesting, despite its faults. Not going to praise it in tongue baths like some of those old survival horror gatekeepers love to do, but I’m not going to burn down its house either. I’m not really wanting fixed-camera survival horror to come back, I think the indie scene has that covered if you want it. Just go in with the expectations that it’s going to suck for at least the first 30 minutes as you get used to everything. Aim your shotgun up for the head when a zombie gets close, always do the kind thing and help out your fellow S.T.A.R.S. members, and maybe play as Jill first.

Maybe me throwing my money at the screen will convince Capcom to make the Resident Evil 2 Remake  :3

Anyways, it's still the best RE game imo. Still holds up very well even after all these years. Play it if you want a challenge, or if you want to understand why all the old fans want to see this style return.

New to the franchise and want to start with the first game? I wouldn't suggest doing that. "Why?" you may say. Please read on

!! CONTAINS SPOILERS !!

You start off in a mansion with no introductions as far as gameplay or controls go, so if you haven't played any RE titles before, it will most likely leave you thinking "what the *beep* do I do now?" 
The mansion is MASSIVE, or at least it feels that way because it's structured like a fricking maze. No matter how many times I've walked down the same halls going from A to B, I manage to get lost along the way. This could also be because of the camera angles this game offers. Yes, ladies and gentlemen, we need to talk about the camera angles.

If you have played any of the newer RE titles whether it's first-person or third-person over the shoulder view, you WILL have a hard time getting used to the fixed camera angles you have in this game. So, basically, you see your character as if you were watching a CCTV footage - I'm not kidding. Once you enter a room you will see the room (and yourself) from e.g a corner. Now, as you move further into the room, the camera may change to the opposite corner of the room. Because the camera angles keep changing all the time, I tend to walk in a loop where I will walk forwards then the camera angle changes to let's say that opposite corner angle I was talking about, thus I invert my joystick (that is if you are playing with a controller, but I guess it's the same with a keyboard) which then leaves you walking backwards and this loops until you realise that the controls get inverted once the camera angle changes. It's not easy to explain and I don't expect you to understand how the view angles work by the way I phrase it. Let's just put it this way: it sucks. It took me hours getting used to, and quite frankly, it's still not ideal. Especially not when you're running away from a monster or a huge boulder. 

The game also has two different controls options to choose from. I decided to play with the new controls since the original tank controls felt unappealing to me. I won't get more into that, that's for you to decide if you end up buying the game.

As far as the gameplay goes, it's actually pretty good once you get a little further into the story. At first, it feels like a door opening simulator. I have never seen so many locked doors in my life and it feels a bit overwhelming at first, that is until you obtain the keys you need to unlock them. Depending on IF and then WHICH resident evil games you have played before, this game is heavily puzzle-based. Dare I say you're doing puzzles 90% of the time? There's not a lot of action or boss fights (I'll get to that later), it's mostly you walking around trying to figure out how to open that one fricking door. [i]You've been at it for six hours now, you can't figure out how to get that door open, ugh... You're starting to get tired, you want to look it up on the internet but at the same time, you want to figure it out yourself. It leaves you thinking "What am I doing with my life?", [/i]sounds familiar? No? Okay, so I got a little carried away....

The graphics are average. They're either good or bad, just average. For its time, being released in 2015, I think the game looks all right. If you compare the graphics to the 1996 original, I think we can all agree that they did a good job. Audio-wise, the game shines. Scary ominous music 10/10. Something that caught my attention was the footstep sounds - they sound absolutely amazing! Voice acting on the other hand made me laugh a few times. Yup, it's that bad. I get that it's a remaster which heavily focused on improving the graphics, so I won't pick too much on it. The lines are also pretty laugh-worthy and goes somewhat like this, using each other's names in most sentences:
Jill - "Barry!"
Barry - "Jill!"
Jill - "Oh, barry!"
Barry - "Jill, I'm so glad you're alive!"
Barry- "You were almost a jill-sandwich!"
Jill - "You're right, Barry"

Boss fights! They have to be good, right? Meh, most can easily be killed with a few shots. Nothing special, to be fair. The first time you encounter the snake, Yawn, you can just grab the death mask and leave the room. You're not forced to fight the epic snake boss, whether that's a good or bad thing is for you to decide. However, you will encounter Yawn later on, and then you'll be forced to kill it. I believe I killed it with three shots from the grenade launcher if I remember correctly. It was fairly easy, despite the snake being highly intimidating. 

Another boss you will encounter two times is the Tyrant. During my first encounter with him, I shot him four times with my revolver and he died. It felt way too easy, but wait, "didn't you say two encounters?" oh yes, I did. You will fight him again shortly after. Without spoiling the whole scene, it goes pretty much exactly the same way that the Resident Evil 2 remake does. Taking a step away from the *weak* bosses, this game has all the evil creatures you could think of: Zombies; sharks; bees; snakes; spiders; plants; crows; dogs and other creatures I can't put a name on.

[H1]Conclusion[/h1]
[i]Is it a good game? Is it worth it?[/i]
Very much so! Absolutely worth it in my opinion [b]IF[/b] you have played RE before or you're a hardcore fan. Otherwise, the puzzles are way too hard for your average player to figure out on their own. Most of the time you have no idea what you're even looking for or where to even remotely look.
This is a great remake/remaster, and kicks off the franchise strong.

Any more in-depth introduction would defeat its purpose since most of you probably spent your time with the original the same way I did: in a darkened room, nose glued to the screen, on the brink of wetting yourself. That was almost 20 years ago and the series changed quite a bit since then - depending on who you ask, not necessarily for the better. Resident Evil left behind its survival horror roots a long time ago in favor of a more dynamic, action-oriented approach. Ever since you had fans yearning for survival horror to make a return while others embraced the new ways, stating that tank controls and fixed camera angles simply wouldn't hold up anymore. But do they hold up? Short answer: Yup, sure do.

It's funny to see developers jumping through hoops to make their game feel "cinematic" when Resident Evil achieved that feat almost 20 years ago without sacrificing the actual game: Fixed camera angles offer the perfect balance between tension and field of view while the pre-rendered backgrounds provide the eye candy as you creep through the mansion and perforate the undead. And due to the control scheme, forward always remains forward when you move out of the picture. The scarce resources along with your limited inventory keep you on your toes and make sure each encounter stays tense. Resident Evil is a slow-paced game that is supposed to be played with foresight and the controls only emphasize that. All of this can be applied to the REmaster.

As a result, the REmaster also inherits many of the original's problems: Some camera angles don't offer as much visibility as they should and at times you find yourself awkwardly jerking around between pictures. And due to the drastically limited inventory the backtracking is strong in this one. You end up visiting the same locations at least twice since you often enter a new area only to realize that the item you need to solve the next puzzle is resting in your locker at the other end of the mansion. You only get six item slots (or eight respectively) where a piece of paper takes up as much space as a motherfucking shotgun. A more elegant item management system could have prevented many unnecessary trips to Mount Doom and back.

Essentially, REmaster is a tarted up version of REmake for Nintendo's Gamecube. If you're like me and never owned one, the REmaster will make the game feel fresh all over again. But if you already own it for Gamecube, the effect will probably not be as strong. Especially considering that the quality of the remade backgrounds is all over the place. There are times when REmaster will flex its muscles and show off its amazing new lighting, but there are other times when you drag your character through low-res, grainy areas that look like they have been chased through a lanczos filter in Photoshop.

In a way, playing REmaster is like spending time with an old friend you haven't seen in ages. It's been so long that you're not sure whether or not he's still cool or if he ever was cool in the first place. When you finally meet again for a drink, you can tell that he tries to give the impression that nothing has changed, yet you can't help but notice some wrinkles along with the receding hairline. Still, you spend some quality time together and you can confirm that he is cool, even now.

Some people would question whether or not it's worth paying for an HD remake that isn't that HD to begin with. Everyone else is already playing it. Like they should.

[h1] Resident Evil teaches that cinematic doesn't mean uninteractive  [/h1]

In the current zeitgeist of the videogame artform, the current standards call for a certain kind of game design. Filling your game with scenes, linear segments and a certain feel that the interaction was an afterthought. Games are trying to become movies and in such process, they simply forget what made videogames so special: interaction.

[b]I'm not implying that such games shouldn't exist, or that such games are inherently bad[/b] — I'm a Metal Gear Solid fan, for fuck's sake. But I also do think that there's a model where they apply such elements without putting any thought on how to properly make the experience justifiable as a game. "Cinematic" became a really marketable adjective, but I don't think any of these recent cutscene focused games are the prime example of this quality just because they have a lot of dialogues and film-like photography. If I'm honest, [b] the most "cinematic" game I have ever played is the one you are looking for opinions right now: Resident Evil Remake. [/b]

Due to the fact this title doesn't force you to watch Hollywood inspired scenes, some people might question my statement. And these people should maybe take some time to watch more films, especially Sam Raimi, Alfred Hitchcock or George Romero's films. [b]Resident Evil Remake is the master of gamifying the experience of watching a horror thriller film through the clever usage of a philosophy the title coined: the so called "survival horror" experience.[/b] Akin to the classic Evil Dead, you are forced to explore an uncharted, lethal environment full of uncertainity. You have limited inventory slots, limited resources and the enemies you are facing are quite relentless. This game will show you how people in the 2000s viewed zombies: flesh dolls that hunt you regardless of how many shots you fired at them; it takes a lot of resources to effectively deal with them.

If you take the wrong choices, you might probably need to restart the game rather early... because even the saving system requires you to use a limited item. It never gets frustrating because the only part of the game [b]you are given full player agency and freedom to experiment is the early segments[/b] (it gets linear and less likely for you to screw up in the last levels). Still, you are always exploring, room after room, with a gun in your hand and a lot of fear of what will appear next. This game hides surprises and plays around with making you familiar with ambients to subvert this notion later, while presenting challenges in unexpected ways. Resident Evil isn't as disturbing as Silent Hill or Fatal Frame, but it's constantly a despair fest, where you are always picking resources and planning your inventory so you can travel through corridors without falling into the mansion's deadly traps. It's the apex of the classic "haunted mansion" trope, even if it avoids supernatural explanations.

This is the first part of the "survival horror" experience, and it's where you might feel frustrated and overwhelmed. However, do not give up! The second part is where you find some kind of overpowering resource, which you can abuse to dominate the game and show those zombies what you are made of. Do you remember when Ash found the shotgun in Evil Dead? You'll feel just like him when you find RE1's shotgun. You will become an overpowered action hero that is throughly able to deal with the threats that oppressed you for so long; that is, until the game throws at you new enemies, traps and puzzles. It's a constant dance of being underpowered and overpowered and it's addicting. [b]It's a masterclass on building tension, giving you consistent pay-offs and surprising you like a classic horror film.[/b]

One might ask himself about the replay value, due to the fact most of the surprises won't have the same effect if you know the mansion. [b]Resident Evil answers this by rewarding players who know the layout with unlockables, new game modes and the fact you have two campaigns.[/b] While you are exploring the same basic environment, choosing between Chris and Jill alters a lot of the resources, gameplay elements and choices you are forced into. Playing at least two times to witness different situations and twists is totally worth it — Chris being the [b]pure ludonarrative path[/b], where you are given [b]total agency of how you explore the mansion, and the game is tougher[/b]; Jill being the more [b]"linear"[/b] path, where you have [b]more resources and you don't need the same amount of backtracking and inventory management[/b], thus making the exploration a bit more of a traditional videogame since you won't need to clear your path or worry about coming back all that much.

And as a remake, it plays around a lot with the idea of [b]surprising the hardcore fan who has played the originals, changing a lot of the surprises and mixing a bit of the mansion's layout.[/b] New mechanics are added and they make the game even harder than it originally was. They also fix a lot of the issues the first game had, such as the underwhelming cave segment, the awful shark "bossfight" while adding a bit more of narrative to spice things up. I'll just say a name: [b]Lisa Trevor[/b], and you'll know what I mean when you get there. It also improves a bit on the controls, allowing you to use the analogue stick and giving you an option if you are not a fan of tank controls.

I'm more of a Chris fan because of how it plays out more akin to "living" a horror film, but both campaigns still feature the same core experience to some degree. Got around this one because I really wanted to try 4's remake, which means I rushed through the original PS1 Resident Evil and then decided to rush through this one too. But I couldn't just rush this, because [b]Resident Evil Remake is a true masterpiece and I feel very compelled to play this until there's no more content to be found.[/b] I already have 50 hours, and this game lasts like, 15~20 hours in your first run. [b] Your run can be optimized up to 2 hours or something if you do play it a lot, and it's just joyful. If you enjoy game design and haven't played this, I don't know what you are doing. This is a purchasable evidence that you can take movie elements and translate into a truly interactive and immersive game. Play it right now![/b]

Resident Evil is a classic fixed-camera horror game, originally released for the Playstation 1, extensively remade for the Nintendo Gamecube and now re-released for PC. As a member of S.T.A.R.S., a special division of the Raccoon City Police, the player participates in an investigation of a series of gruesome murders taking place in the remote Arklay Mountains. After being ambushed and overwhelmed in the woods they are forced to retreat and take shelter in a seemingly abandoned mansion.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Throughout the game the player has to explore and navigate the many rooms of the mansion as well as solving puzzles and finding keys to progress. Outside of a map keeping track which rooms already have been visited and which doors remain locked, there isn't much explicit guidance which can lead to a lot of time spent simply exploring and picking up various puzzle items without immediately knowing how to use them. Examining an item from the inventory menu can often reveal greater insight into how to use it, but even then it may not be obvious until later in the game.
Much of the game is spent backtracking through the mansion. The player character's inventory is of very limited capacity and has to fit weapons, healing items and puzzle pieces alike. It's not possible to carry all of them at once, making it necessary to stash some in item boxes, which can be found in save rooms. The player has to decide what to make room for and what to leave behind in order to be able to pick up more items as they keep exploring or come back for them at a later point.
While slowly moving from room to room the player will encounter many zombies roaming the halls, who will attempt to grab and bite them. Combat generally is as simple as pointing a weapon at an enemy and shooting until they drop to the ground, however there are caveats. The amount of ammo to be found throughout the game is limited and sometimes a room may not be worth the expense to clean out for a variety of reasons, including that zombies could come back stronger if they aren't appropriately dealt with. It is up to the player to decide whether they want to clear out a route for good or if they only want to quickly pass through, possibly using up a healing item instead of ammo if they get injured. Room for movement is generally tight and claustrophobia-inducing, especially with the control scheme that a fixed-camera perspective enforces. Since the player isn't always able to see what's directly in front of them, some encounters might be difficult to gauge visually, so forethought into how to approach an encounter as well as sometimes just retreating pays off.
The game can be saved only at typewriters placed throughout the game, using up ink ribbons which can be picked up and stored like any other item. Enough of them are placed in the game to allow comfortably frequent saving, if spread out between every other point of progress.

[h1]Storytelling[/h1]
The game allows to choose from two playable characters who apart from having their respective gameplay differences, also have unique cutscenes and interactions with other characters. The main plot remains largely unaffected by this however.

Cutscene interruptions are fairly rare and usually only happen after major progress milestones. Most of the lore is conveyed through diaries and logs left behind in the mansion.

[h1]Remaster Differences and Technical Issues[/h1]
The original game used a tank control scheme (D-PAD Up = Walk Foward, D-PAD Left and Right = Turn Character), which makes moving around initially feel rather awkward and takes a while to get used to. However the game's encounters have been designed with this in mind and are decently playable after some adjustment period.
The remaster added modern omni-directional analogue stick movement, which generally is much easier to control, however due to the fixed-camera perspective the walk direction corresponding to the stick direction can suddenly change when transitioning between screens. Both control schemes can be used at any time by simply switching the thumb between D-PAD and stick on the fly. It should be noted however that using analogue movement controls can trivialize portions of the game, since they weren't expected to exist back when the game was originally conceived.

Widescreen support has been added with the remaster, however it may be worth considering disabling it. The original pre-rendered backgrounds were made for an aspect ratio of 4:3 and in order to make them fill the screen the game zooms in on them and pans the screen according to where the player character currently is visible. This can look very distracting because the perspective isn't properly preserved anymore. The game allows sticking with the original 4:3 ratio which will add black bars to the sides of the screen, but have the actual image remain in a static position, as well as allowing a wider field of vision, because the entire image is shown at all times.

Some people have encountered a "slow motion" bug, with the game randomly stuttering and playing poorly, it appears to not be known what causes this and how to fix it when it happens. I personally have never encountered it in my entire playthrough, but it may be something to look out for.

New costume options for the player characters have been added, one each, modelled after their appearances in Resident Evil 5. They can be selected before starting a new game.

[h1]Final Judgement[/h1]
I've only recently discovered Resident Evil for myself, and while you can certainly tell that it's a product of its time, it still conveyed an intriguing atmosphere as I was uncovering the mystery of the mansion. The fixed camera perspective might be somewhat frustrating to deal with at times, such as getting injured when you cannot really see what is moaning and swiping at you immediately in front, but it also brings a certain creepy mood to the environment that would have been lost if you were allowed full control over the camera.
Some of the puzzles can take a while to figure out, often because it can be a long time before an item actually becomes relevant or because you forgot to properly examine it, but the solutions themselves are not so otherworldly that it is ever a requirement to bust out a walkthrough if you pay enough attention to the hints that the game already provides you with.
The visuals of the environment have aged incredibly well. Although while under strict scrutiny you can tell that the backgrounds are pre-rendered and that live-rendered characters stick slightly out, it is practically never noticeable while playing normally (unless you play in the bad widescreen mode). This game made the most out of its old rendering technique back in the and still holds up rather well because of it.

Talking about how good Resident Evil HD Remaster is, it is like talking about how good was Bruce Lee’s “The Big Boss”: you might not like them, but you cannot deny how important and instrumental they were in advancing and popularizing their respective genres. 

The classic Resident Evil has stood the test of time: there are some aspects of the game that are great(ly terrifying) even today, such as the dread-filled atmosphere as you wait to see what horrors are lurking beyond the old wooden door of the next room, claustrophobic and limiting movement and combat system, nice puzzle sections to ease the player a bit before the next big scare, two overlapping single-player campaigns that flesh out the story (no pun intended), and who can forget the nerve-racking resurrections of crimson heads caused by your neglect, and undead pooches! There are also some duds in the game that time has run over like critics did over Stephen King’s drug-fueled first and only movie directorial debut: camera switching madly and constantly changing perception to add the additional element of fright to the player today seems more irritating than enjoyable, let alone scary; the story’s backdrop and how the T-Virus was created in the past are more interesting and serious then the entirety of the current campy story the game is showing. The first Resident Evil game never was perfect; it was created as an omage to the schlocky horror movie classics of the past by the original developers.

But, to their credit, Capcom has given it all and birthed a new remake of this survival horror classic that polishes the graphics and the dialogue, while leaving everything else in its pristine, antiquated condition. 2D backgrounds the player is traversing are looking better and chilling than ever before, 3D models of the protagonists and monsters have been greatly enriched and sharpened, while the corny dialogue of the original game was also overhauled with a more serious, if not easily forgettable note in mind. Heck, even the simple yet effective PS1 soundtrack got a nice and equally serious Botox injection. This has resulted in a strikingly beautiful and rugged game that exudes atmosphere of elegance and fear in every playthrough and screenshot the community makes. As for leaving the crutches the original game had, this is a beloved game among players so fiddling with the core, beating heart of this Resident Evil would not end well, but one cannot help and imagine what wonder or a catastrophe of the game we would get if Capcom had more faith and courage and reworked everything. Luckily, they showed their iron will with a completely reimagined Resident Evil 2, but that is a story for another time.

Some things age like fine wine, and those things are always in a vast minority and should be cherished. Such is the case with the Resident Evil HD Remaster (good lord that prolonged title though), a game that spawned a series that has been frightening players for more than 20 years now, with a varying degree of success. This game is and will remain a captivating shiny, red and imperfect jewel of the horror survival genre that everyone should play.

Resident Evil teaches that cinematic doesn't mean uninteractive.

In the current zeitgeist of the videogame artform, the current standards call for a certain kind of game design. Filling your game with scenes, linear segments and a certain feel that the interaction was an afterthought. Games are trying to become movies and in such process, they simply forget what made videogames so special: interaction.

I'm not implying that such games shouldn't exist, or that such games are inherently bad — I'm a Metal Gear Solid fan, for F's sake. But I also do think that there's a model where they apply such elements without putting any thought on how to properly make the experience justifiable as a game. "Cinematic" became a really marketable adjective, but I don't think any of these recent cutscene focused games are the prime example of this quality just because they have a lot of dialogues and film-like photography. If I'm honest, the most "cinematic" game I have ever played is the one you are looking for opinions right now: Resident Evil Remake.

Due to the fact this title doesn't force you to watch Hollywood inspired scenes, some people might question my statement. And these people should maybe take some time to watch more films, especially Sam Raimi, Alfred Hitchcock or George Romero's films. Resident Evil Remake is the master of gamifying the experience of watching a horror thriller film through the clever usage of a philosophy the title coined: the so called "survival horror" experience. Akin to the classic Evil Dead, you are forced to explore an uncharted, lethal environment full of uncertainity. You have limited inventory slots, limited resources and the enemies you are facing are quite relentless. This game will show you how people in the 2000s viewed zombies: flesh dolls that hunt you regardless of how many shots you fired at them; it takes a lot of resources to effectively deal with them.

If you take the wrong choices, you might probably need to restart the game rather early... because even the saving system requires you to use a limited item. It never gets frustrating because the only part of the game you are given full player agency and freedom to experiment is the early segments (it gets linear and less likely for you to screw up in the last levels). Still, you are always exploring, room after room, with a gun in your hand and a lot of fear of what will appear next. This game hides surprises and plays around with making you familiar with ambients to subvert this notion later, while presenting challenges in unexpected ways. Resident Evil isn't as disturbing as Silent Hill or Fatal Frame, but it's constantly a despair fest, where you are always picking resources and planning your inventory so you can travel through corridors without falling into the mansion's deadly traps. It's the apex of the classic "haunted mansion" trope, even if it avoids supernatural explanations.

This is the first part of the "survival horror" experience, and it's where you might feel frustrated and overwhelmed. However, do not give up! The second part is where you find some kind of overpowering resource, which you can abuse to dominate the game and show those zombies what you are made of. Do you remember when Ash found the shotgun in Evil Dead? You'll feel just like him when you find RE1's shotgun. You will become an overpowered action hero that is throughly able to deal with the threats that oppressed you for so long; that is, until the game throws at you new enemies, traps and puzzles. It's a constant dance of being underpowered and overpowered and it's addicting. It's a masterclass on building tension, giving you consistent pay-offs and surprising you like a classic horror film.

One might ask himself about the replay value, due to the fact most of the surprises won't have the same effect if you know the mansion. Resident Evil answers this by rewarding players who know the layout with unlockables, new game modes and the fact you have two campaigns. While you are exploring the same basic environment, choosing between Chris and Jill alters a lot of the resources, gameplay elements and choices you are forced into. Playing at least two times to witness different situations and twists is totally worth it — Chris being the pure ludonarrative path, where you are given total agency of how you explore the mansion, and the game is tougher; Jill being the more "linear" path, where you have more resources and you don't need the same amount of backtracking and inventory management, thus making the exploration a bit more of a traditional videogame since you won't need to clear your path or worry about coming back all that much.

And as a remake, it plays around a lot with the idea of surprising the hardcore fan who has played the originals, changing a lot of the surprises and mixing a bit of the mansion's layout. New mechanics are added and they make the game even harder than it originally was. They also fix a lot of the issues the first game had, such as the underwhelming cave segment, the awful shark "bossfight" while adding a bit more of narrative to spice things up. I'll just say a name: Lisa Trevor, and you'll know what I mean when you get there. It also improves a bit on the controls, allowing you to use the analogue stick and giving you an option if you are not a fan of tank controls.

I'm more of a Chris fan because of how it plays out more akin to "living" a horror film, but both campaigns still feature the same core experience to some degree. Resident Evil Remake is a true masterpiece and I feel very compelled to play this until there's no more content to be found. I already have +20 hours, and this game lasts like, 10-12 hours in your first run. Your run can be optimized up to 2 hours or something if you do play it a lot, and it's just joyful. If you enjoy game design and haven't played this, I don't know what you are doing. This is a purchasable evidence that you can take movie elements and translate into a truly interactive and immersive game. Play it right now!

Fantastic remake, and one of the best survival horror games ever made.

Graphics are amazing. Even today, everything looks beautiful, with incredible attention to detail, atmosphere, and lighting. The Spencer Mansion feels more alive and immersive than ever. Character and enemy models received a huge upgrade compared to the original game, and the animations are much smoother and more detailed. The visual presentation strikes a perfect balance between preserving the original style and modernizing it. It's almost sad that you can't rotate the camera to fully appreciate the beautiful environments. Also, the new cinematics are great; they strangely feel more real than the FMV ones of the original.

Sound effects are fantastic. Every footstep, creaking door, distant growl, thunder roar, and environmental noise contributes to the atmosphere. The game constantly keeps you on edge, making you wonder what might be waiting around the next corner. The soundtrack is excellent, sometimes using music to build tension and other times relying on silence to make the environment even more unsettling. Voice acting is significantly improved compared to the original release; also, the dialogues feel more realistic and grounded.

Gameplay is great and incredibly engaging. About the controls, the game offers both the original tank controls and a modern control scheme, allowing players to choose whichever they prefer. I couldn't get used to the "modern" controls. After playing the original, these new controls felt so strange and clunky to use, so I went back to the original controls. Regardless of your choice, the game is built around deliberate movement, resource management, and careful decision-making rather than fast-paced action.

Combat still has the same feeling, simple on the surface but surprisingly strategic. The defensive weapons addition is a great one. 

Exploration is still one of the game's greatest strengths. The mansion has a new layout but keeps the original locations and upgrades some of the weaker places that it had, along with some new great places. Same with the puzzles, keeping some original ones with a few twists, upgrading and changing the weaker ones, and adding new interesting ones.

The enemies remain the same, great overall, but the addition of the Crimson Head system (zombies that are not burned or decapitated can eventually return as faster and more dangerous enemies) adds another layer of strategy and decision-making to the game. 

The story remains almost the same, with some additions and more context, but overall, it's great.

The only bad thing I can say about the game is... doors; you can't skip the annoying animations, like in the original. I know... it adds to the tension and atmosphere and all, and in the first playthrough, it's ok, but after that it's just annoying as F! Thank God you can use mods to solve that problem!

In short, a fantastic remake and one of the finest examples of survival horror ever created. It preserves everything that made the original special while improving nearly every aspect of the experience. If you enjoy exploration, resource management, puzzles, and atmospheric horror, this game is absolutely worth playing. Give it a chance, and you will have a fantastic experience.

The Birthplace of Survival Horror - A Review of Resident Evil

Overall Rating: 9.75/10

Resident Evil stands as one of the most important survival horror games ever created, and its modern release preserves everything that made it legendary while subtly refining the experience. Set within the infamous Spencer Mansion, the game is a masterclass in tension, atmosphere, and deliberate pacing. Rather than relying on constant action, it builds fear through confinement, uncertainty, and the ever-present threat of the unknown. This is survival horror in its purest, most disciplined form.

Visual Design and Atmosphere: 9.5/10
The mansion remains one of gaming’s most iconic locations. Pre-rendered backgrounds are richly detailed, filled with shadowy hallways, decaying rooms, and unsettling stillness. Every environment feels carefully composed, using fixed camera angles to frame danger just outside the player’s view. Lighting and environmental detail elevate the setting into something oppressive yet elegant, making exploration both mesmerizing and nerve-wracking. The mansion itself feels hostile, as if every corridor and room is actively working against your survival.

Story and Narrative: 9/10
Resident Evil tells its story with restraint and confidence, allowing the player to uncover its secrets through exploration rather than direct explanation. Journal entries, environmental details, and subtle story beats piece together a slow, unsettling descent into biological horror. The tragedy of the mansion’s past reveals itself gradually, while the larger Umbrella conspiracy looms in the background with pulpy, genre-defining flair. The narrative works hand in hand with the gameplay, reinforcing tension and discovery while naturally supporting the game’s deliberate survival-focused design.

Gameplay and Survival Mechanics: 9.5/10
This is where Resident Evil defines the genre. Limited resources, deliberate movement, and careful inventory management create constant tension. The presence of item boxes provides strategic relief, turning backtracking into a thoughtful risk-versus-reward system rather than pure frustration. Combat is intentionally stiff, reinforcing vulnerability and making every encounter a decision rather than a reflex. Exploration, puzzle-solving, and survival are perfectly intertwined.

Sound Design and Music: 10/10
The soundscape is nothing short of iconic. Ambient silence is frequently more terrifying than any musical cue, broken only by distant footsteps, creaking floors, or the sudden moan of the undead. When music does surface, it’s deliberate and unforgettable—haunting melodies that heighten tension without overwhelming it. The soundtrack understands restraint, using music as punctuation rather than constant accompaniment.

Immersion and Replayability: 10/10
Resident Evil rewards multiple playthroughs through alternate characters, routes, and item placements. Familiarity never dulls the experience; instead, it deepens appreciation for its design. Speed runs, challenge modes, and mastery of the mansion layout keep the game engaging long after the first completion.

Conclusion: 9.75/10
Resident Evil is a benchmark for survival horror, proving that fear doesn’t come from excess—but from control. Its careful balance of atmosphere, mechanics, and sound design creates a slow-burning tension few games have ever matched. Every door opened feels earned, every bullet spent feels costly, and every moment inside the mansion feels dangerous.

Final Verdict:
A masterclass in survival horror design, Resident Evil remains as effective today as it was at release. Its deliberate pacing, oppressive atmosphere, and interconnected systems work in harmony to create an experience where tension is constant and every decision matters. Few games understand fear through limitation as completely—or as confidently—as this one.

A remastered rerelease of the 2002 remake of Resident Evil, available for the first time on PC. Spoilers: It's great. The game's graphics and ambience were nothing short of astounding in 2002, and with only minor alterations still look incredible in 2018. Technically speaking, the port runs flawlessly. A new, alternative control scheme has been added for those that can't stand tank controls. There's no excuse not to pick up and play one of the greatest horror games of all time.

[h1]STORY[/h1]
Resident Evil's story is in a slightly surreal realm, its dialogue and occasionally bizarre character reactions treading the line of 'so bad it's good'. This is nothing new to anybody who's played any other Resident Evil game. In 1998, the S.T.A.R.S. Alpha team is sent to investigate the disappearance of the Bravo team, who themselves were investigating a string of cannibalistic murders. Finding Bravo Team's helicopter crashed in the forest and several of their number dead, our heroes quickly find themselves menaced by strange dogs and chased through the woods into a mysterious mansion. At this point the player chooses whether to play as Chris Redfield or Jill Valentine, with the protagonist not chosen quickly becoming lost in the mansion.

[h1]GAMEPLAY[/h1]
RE's gameplay will be familiar to those who grew up in the 1990s - you explore an undead-infested mansion with prerendered graphics and fixed camera angles, using either the original "tank controls" or the newly added relative controls, which allow for far more nimble control of your character. (Take note, the new control scheme allows your character to be so much more nimble that the game's level of fear and menace may be compromised. Whether that's a good or a bad thing is entirely up to you.)

Weapons are hard to come by and even harder to keep loaded - a very limited inventory space (even more so depending which playable character you choose) and scarce pickings for ammo in the game world ensure that clearing the mansion of zombies is basically a pipe dream. Running and skilfully dodging the undead soon become the norm, with killing relegated to zombies which are occupying major thoroughfares and shortcuts you find yourself travelling often.

Adding to the menace is the threat that killed zombies may resurrect, mutating into lightning-fast variants known as Crimson Heads after a certain amount of real-world time has passed, or after certain plot events. Crimson Heads are fierce and relentless, and their creation can only be prevented by getting a lucky headshot and destroying the head of the zombie or by burning its corpse. This of course requires kerosene (which is limited and takes up valuable inventory space). Many factors go into the consideration of whether killing any given zombie is actually a good idea or will make life harder for you down the road.

[h1]PRESENTATION[/h1]
This is where Resident Evil truly shines. The pre-rendered graphics are almost photorealistic, creating a real and constant sense of looming terror throughout the mansion. The sound design works hand in hand with the graphical fidelity, with mysterious creaks and thunderclaps piercing the eeriely silent night at all the wrong times. Generally speaking, Resident Evil games aren't exactly survival horror games anymore, in either the survival or the horror sense. RE1 is both, remaining to this day one of the scariest games on the market (thanks in part to its impeccable timing and restraint when it comes to actually unleashing jumpscares versus holding back and biding its time).

[h1]CONCLUSION[/h1]
REmake is one of the great classics of gaming - one of those rare games that absolutely everyone with any interest in the genre should play. If you haven't already, rectify that. It's more than worth full price, so any discount you can get it for is a steal in my books.

To this day, this game still looks beautiful. The static backgrounds are so detailed and the characters do not feel out of place. They feel like they are part of the environment, not pasted in. The best way to play this game is NOT in widescreen but in the original 4:3 aspect ratio. The reason being is because in widescreen, they stretch the width a bit but also cut off the top and bottom of the scenery. Because of this, you lose a lot of detail in the environment, along with the background not being as sharp and crisp as it is in 4:3 mode. 4:3 mode lets you see the original scene as it was intended.

The story is great and very engaging. And for those that played the original game before the remake, the main story is there but enhanced with new stories that add to the lore, add to the story, and make the game even more engaging. Many puzzles from the original are there, but are enhanced so that those that know the solution still have to figure them out.

Puzzles are not overly difficult nor too easy. They are intriguing and fun to figure out. As much as I like the RE2 Remake, this game definitely is tops of all the Resident Evils out there in my humble opinion. Some may not feel that way, but you can feel the love and compassion the developers put into this game; how they fleshed out the story, how the architecture of the environments feel so organic and not out-of-place, how the game-play is fun to do and feels "just right", and the music and ambient sounds just create such an environment of tension. Since you move from scene to scene, it "hides" zombies on purpose, making you have to possibly move slowly rather than trying to run through each room because there could be zombie right around the next corner you turn at and move onto another scene. You as the player need to be aware of the environment, the sounds you hear which give clues as to where zombies are at, and just so many other factors that the developers and writers ensured made this game fun to play, over and over again.

Get it! It's worth it!

The survival horror classic that started the entire genre. But what is it exactly that made this game so great? 

Now I don't wanna talk about the story in case someone hasn't played this yet, so I'll be focusing on other things in this review, that being the actual gameplay. 

Well, first of all, the atmosphere. It's always there, starting from the first minutes of the game. The spooky dark ambient soundtrack, the first person door opening scenes. You'll never know what's lurking on the other side of the door and it can lead to your death countless times before you start to get the hang of the "tank controls". 

That leads to the next thing that makes this game the memorable classic it still is to this day, which exactly are the controls. Basically, you press up (W on PC, obviously) to go forward regardless of the camera angle, which keeps changing all the time and messes with your mind at first. Believe me, if you've never played this game before, you will have a hard time getting used to them at first, but once you do, it's not really a hard game, and it feels so rewarding to finally beat it. Now there is an alternate control scheme for this remaster, but imo, it just made it harder to play. Honestly, I couldn't really figure out how you're supposed to play the game with this new control scheme, even though I was new to the series. Everything was just the opposite from what it should be, or I'm just stupid. Whatever the case is, the only useful thing I found about the alternate controls was that you don't have to press shift to run, but that's not much so I'd rather play this with the og tank controls anytime. Besides, in a game like RE, running automatically can often lead to your death more easily, or that's how I felt anyway when I tried that control scheme. Not for me, that's all I can say.

Now the most important thing that makes this game the unique piece it is, and the number #1 rule of the game you could say, is that everything is limited: ammo, saves, item slots (prepare to use item boxes a lot, you only have 8 item slots), gas (you need that and the lighter to burn the corpses so they won't turn into Crimson Heads. Now what is a Crimson Head? That you'll have to find out yourself if you don't already know it, but a little hint for you: you might not want to find out, so I'd recommend to just burn every corpse you can). You use "ink ribbons" to save your game. These are items that can be found throughout the mansion, but like I said, they're limited too. So once you'll remember to not use too much ammo or too many ink ribbons, you should be fine (when you get used to the controls first, that is, whichever control scheme you prefer). Keep in mind that this is a remaster of the 2002 GameCube remake and not the original game. I've never played the original one and I had to restart this game once because I was wasting too much ammo and using too many ink ribbons on my first playthrough. 

And last but not least, the thing I enjoyed the most: The puzzles. Some of them are easy, but some of them really make you use your brain. I admit that I was stuck for hours multiple times during this game, but that's what made it an interesting experience for me. A lot of these puzzles require quite a bit of backtracking due to the limited item slots. 

So, my final verdict for this game, if you haven't played a lot of horror games and you want to start with the classics, here it is for you. A true masterpiece of the genre, I'd recommend this to anyone. Even if you're not into horror yet, who knows, it might change your mind? Give it a chance I'd say, I enjoyed it a lot and I can totally understand why it has such a huge fanbase. Highly recommended if you're even the slightest bit interested about the survival horror genre or zombie games in general.

Resident Evil HD Remaster is one of those games that proves a great horror game does not need modern graphics or complicated mechanics to be scary. Originally released as the 2002 remake of the first Resident Evil, this HD version gives the game a visual upgrade while keeping almost everything that made the original so good.

The Spencer Mansion is still the highlight of the experience. The mansion feels mysterious, dangerous and surprisingly believable. The fixed camera angles work really well because they constantly leave you wondering what is waiting around the next corner. You might hear a zombie before you see it, or walk into a room without knowing what is hiding just outside the camera.

The game also does a great job with survival horror. You have limited ammunition, limited inventory space and a limited number of healing items, so you have to think about how you approach each situation. You cannot simply kill every enemy you come across. Sometimes it is smarter to run away and save your resources.

The Crimson Heads are a great example of this. Killing a zombie does not always mean it is gone forever. If you do not deal with its body properly, it can come back as a much faster and more dangerous enemy. This makes you think carefully about which enemies are worth killing and which ones you should avoid.

The puzzles and exploration are also a big part of the experience. The puzzles are not particularly difficult, but they encourage you to explore the mansion and remember where you have been. The limited inventory can be frustrating at times, especially when you find an important item but have no room to carry it, but it also makes you plan your trips more carefully.

The HD upgrade looks good overall. The environments are sharper, the character models look better and widescreen support makes the game feel much more comfortable on modern televisions. However, it is still very obvious that this is a game from 2002. Some backgrounds and cutscenes look dated, but the strong art direction helps the game hold up surprisingly well.

The controls can take some getting used to, especially if you are accustomed to modern Resident Evil games. You can choose between the original style controls and a newer control option, but the fixed camera can sometimes make the newer controls confusing. Once you get used to the classic controls, they actually work quite well with the game's design.

The story is simple but entertaining, with zombies, Umbrella, secret experiments and plenty of classic Resident Evil moments. Some of the dialogue is cheesy, but honestly, that is part of the charm.

Resident Evil HD Remaster does have some flaws. There is quite a bit of backtracking, the inventory system can become annoying and the controls feel dated compared with modern games. However, these problems are also part of what gives the game its old school survival horror identity.

Overall, Resident Evil HD Remaster is still an excellent game. It may take some patience to get used to its slower pace and older design, but once you get into it, the atmosphere and tension are incredibly effective.

It does not need to completely reinvent Resident Evil because the 2002 remake was already fantastic. The HD Remaster simply gives that experience a cleaner presentation for modern players.

Final Score: 8.5 out of 10

If you enjoy survival horror, Resident Evil HD Remaster is absolutely worth playing. It is old fashioned in some ways, but its atmosphere, exploration and resource management still hold up extremely well.
